item.title: Stop Apologizing for Everything
item.description:
Shame

Stop Apologizing for Everything

When saying “I’m sorry” becomes self-erasure.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic apologizing is often a preemptive defense against shame.
  • There's a real difference between healthy shame and toxic shame.
  • Notice the urge to apologize and ask yourself whether you did anything wrong.

If we learned anything from the COVID-19 pandemic, it was that Zoom calls would, for most people, replace live face-to-face meetings. With it came an implied list of virtual rules the likes of which would make Emily Post blush. Chief among them was beginning every question with a polite recognition that began with the phrase, “Apologies if you covered this already, but I’m curious to know…” It was as if SARS-CoV-2 had brought with it a co-infection of polite etiquette.

But apologizing constantly—especially when you haven’t done anything wrong—isn’t politeness. It’s shame in disguise. When shame tells you that you are the problem, apologizing becomes a preemptive defense. You say “I’m sorry” before anyone can accuse you. It feels like humility, but it's actually self-erasure.

The Link Between Self-Erasure and Chronic People-Pleasing

Much of the research on self-erasure links it to chronic people-pleasing, in which a disproportionate external focus leads to disconnection from your authentic self. This draws on trauma research on the “fawn” response. Initially described by Pete Walker, a psychotherapist specializing in complex PTSD, “fawning” is a response to a threat in which the individual becomes more appealing to the threat—mirroring someone else’s desire to diffuse conflict and find safety by surrendering their own boundaries.

Fawning is considered the fourth F in the fight/flight/freeze response. Fight-or-flight dates back to Walter Cannon’s (1915) work on the sympathetic nervous system. Freeze was introduced later by Dr. Peter Levine. The three Fs were given a home in 1995, when neuroscientist Stephen Porges first published his polyvagal theory. Deb Dana, a clinician who worked with Porges, translated the theory into the Polyvagal Ladder metaphor, a more usable therapeutic construct with three rungs:

  1. Top Rung: ventral vagal (safe and social).
  2. Middle Rung: sympathetic (fight or flight).
  3. Bottom Rung: dorsal vagal (freeze/shutdown).

How Fawning Fits Into the Polyvagal Theory

Where does fawning fit? It doesn’t get its own rung. Generally, it’s described as sitting at the intersection of the freeze/shutdown state, with an extra dollop of appeasement laid on top, since it involves both the immobilization of the dorsal vagal shutdown and a strategic, socially oriented move to placate the threat.

What does this look like in real life? You apologize for having an opinion, for taking up space, for existing in a way that might inconvenience someone else. Here's the distinction worth making: apologizing for something you did wrong is healthy shame doing its job. Apologizing for who you are—that's toxic shame playing the part of the officious server, hovering before a table of diners who haven’t opened their menus yet, poised to apologize for making them wait.

Overcoming Reflexive Apologies

Tying it all together: the shame-driven, boundary-blurring apology you offer up reflexively is literally what fawning looks like physiologically. A nervous system that dropped toward shutdown but is using an appeasing behavior to climb back up toward safety rather than genuine repair of something that went wrong.

Here’s your practice. Next time you feel the urge to apologize, pause. Ask yourself: Did I actually do something wrong, or am I apologizing for taking up space?

Because you were never meant to stand on the sidelines when you earned a seat at the table.

item.title: Why Parents Are Shocked When an Adult Child Goes No Contact
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Why Parents Are Shocked When an Adult Child Goes No Contact

Reconciliation isn't as likely when parents dismiss their child's experience.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Parents' denial or defensiveness often blinds them to signs of a strained relationship.
  • Estrangement usually follows years of hurt and failed attempts to resolve conflict, not one incident.
  • Adult children may withdraw gradually, but parents may misinterpret distance as independence or busyness.
Source: SHVETS production/Pexels

Why are so many parents shocked or blindsided when an adult child goes no contact?

Many parents describe estrangement as coming completely out of the blue. They may insist they had no idea there was a problem, point out that they weren't perfect but were good parents, or struggle to understand how a family that seemed close could end up here.

Sometimes confusion is genuine, but being unaware of the problem doesn't mean there weren’t any signs. Parents may experience interactions differently than their adult child, particularly when certain family patterns feel normal to them.

It’s also possible for “I have no idea why” to be a form of denial. If a parent can't—or won't—see what went wrong, it's easier to blame the therapist, social media, or the adult child than to consider their own role.

Why Parents May Not See Estrangement Coming

Estrangement is rarely the result of an isolated incident. It typically follows years of hurtful experiences, disappointments, conflicts, and attempts to improve a difficult relationship (Agllias, 2016, 2018; Scharp, 2016; Scharp et al., 2015).

Parents may genuinely believe their child never communicated a problem. However, if that was the case, one needs to consider whether the parent was willing and emotionally safe to hear them.

An adult child may have tried to talk about what was bothering them, only to have their concerns minimized, explained away, criticized, or turned into an argument. For example, a parent might respond with, “That's not what happened,” “You're too sensitive,” “I was only trying to help,” or “After everything I've done for you.” The parent may have seen this as defending themselves or correcting an unfair accusation, while the child may have concluded there was no point in continuing to bring it up.

This is one reason the complaint that “they never told me there was a problem” can be misleading. The more useful questions are: Did they try to tell me? Did I take them seriously? Could they disagree with me or express hurt without being punished, dismissed, or made responsible for my feelings?

Sometimes, the adult child has been gradually pulling away—withdrawing, sharing less, avoiding certain topics, declining invitations, or becoming increasingly guarded. These changes may be interpreted as independence, busyness, or a phase, rather than the result of a strained relationship.

By the time an adult child cuts ties, they may feel that they have already tried to communicate in every way they know how. The parent may experience the estrangement as sudden; the child may experience it as the end of a very long process. As I wrote in my book Cutting Ties with Your Parents, “In over two decades as a therapist, I’ve yet to encounter anyone who made the decision to cut ties lightly. Adult children typically struggle to resolve their family conflicts for years before calling it quits” (p. 8).

“I Have No Idea” Can Become a Defense

Parents who see themselves as loving and well-intentioned often struggle to accept that their child experienced the relationship as hurtful. That can bring up shame, guilt, grief, and uncertainty.

It can also require reconsidering decades of family history, which is painful. So the mind naturally looks for alternative explanations, such as the adult child was poisoned against them by social media, a therapist, or a partner. Or that the estrangement is due to the adult child's inaccurate memories, selfishness, or ingratitude.

Any of these factors could potentially play a role in an individual situation. But when they become the entire explanation, they can serve another purpose: to keep the parent's own behavior out of the picture.

“But I Was a Good Parent”

One reason estrangement is so painful is that it doesn't only happen when parenting is entirely bad. A parent can love their child deeply, provide for them, make sacrifices, and believe they did their best—and still have behaved in ways that cause significant pain.

Asking whether the parent was “good” or “bad” isn’t particularly helpful. More important is whether the adult child experienced aspects of the relationship as hurtful, dismissive, controlling, or unsafe.

Good intentions and positive memories don’t mean that harm wasn’t caused. An adult child can feel unimportant, controlled, criticized, or unable to be fully themselves even in a family that spends holidays together and talks regularly.

Defensiveness Undermines Reconciliation

The irony is that some parents who want to reconcile respond to estrangement in ways that make reconciliation less likely. For example, if an adult child says, “You didn't respect my boundaries,” and the response is, “That's not true. I've always respected you,” the parent may believe they're setting the record straight. But the adult feels dismissed, which pushes them further away.

Reconciliation requires being willing to hear that the other person experienced the relationship differently. That doesn't mean accepting every accusation as fact, but it does require listening without immediately becoming defensive or dismissive.

Ultimately, you can't repair a relationship while insisting that there's no valid reason for its breakdown. Reconciliation starts with acknowledging that the relationship may not have been what you thought it was.
